title: SDK experience playbook for realtime actions and declarative JSON PRD
body:
Context and motivation:

We ship a hosted streaming API that supports incremental text + structured outputs and first-class tool-calls. Teams building integrations (search, code execution, commerce actions) are repeatedly asking for a predictable SDK surface that: works across unreliable networks (mobile), makes tool-handshake patterns explicit and testable, handles partial/typed JSON without developer pain, and gives clear migration paths as we evolve streaming framing.

This doc proposes an operational PRD: a pragmatic SDK playbook and API contract for realtime action workflows using declarative JSON payloads. The emphasis is developer ergonomics, deterministic failure modes, and observability hooks that map directly to the Console.

Problem statement:

- Current hosted streaming UX leaks framing decisions to clients: ad-hoc partial JSON fragments, inconsistent tool-call lifecycle handling, and opaque retry semantics.
- SDKs implemented per-platform have divergent behaviors: some return raw bytes, others buffer until valid JSON, making cross-platform parity difficult.
- Tool-calling often mixes control frames and user-facing tokens in the same stream, complicating client-side routing and testing.
- Lack of a compact, stable typed-envelope format forces teams to write brittle parsers and brittle code around partial outputs.

Goals (measurable):

1) Define a compact streaming envelope and tool-call lifecycle that SDKs will implement consistently across JS, Python, and mobile (iOS/Android).
2) Reduce integration time: target a 50% reduction in time-to-first-successful-tool-invocation for customer POCs (measured via onboarding surveys + SE notes).
3) Improve developer-observable fidelity: expose token-level source attribution and frame-level telemetry with consistent naming (Console and SDK) so customers can map errors to model/tool/transport.
4) Provide explicit partial/typed-JSON semantics so clients can consume progressive structured output safely (no invalid JSON surprise).

Non-goals:

- Replacing existing bulk / non-streaming REST endpoints.
- Solving every client-side UI pattern — we provide primitives and examples, not full UI components.

User personas:

- Embedded product engineer building an assistant view with tool buttons and progressive hinting (mobile + web).
- Platform engineer at an enterprise wiring Redwood Dedicated into a backend processing pipeline that needs deterministic retry behavior.
- Solutions engineer running customer proof-of-concepts who needs predictable logs and test harnesses.

Design constraints and principles:

- Minimal coupling: control frames (handshake/ack/errors) must be clearly separable from display/content frames.
- Deterministic resumes: resume tokens should be sufficient to recover a consistent application state without re-executing side-effects.

High-level proposal (summary):

1) Streaming envelope: a compact newline-separated envelope where each line is a small JSON object: {"t": "type", "id": "session/frame id", "p": <payload>, "meta": {...}}. Type values include: "delta", "commit", "tool-call", "tool-result", "control", "checkpoint". This keeps framing explicit and easy to parse on low-memory devices.

2) Typed progressive payloads: payloads use a 2-layer encoding for structured parts: text deltas delivered as plain string segments, typed payloads delivered as JSON fragments with an explicit status field {"status":"partial|complete|error","data": <fragment|value>}. SDKs will provide both a stream-of-deltas API and a high-level builder that yields fully assembled typed objects.

3) Tool-call lifecycle: tool-call frames separate intent and execution. A tool invocation is a mini-transaction with frames: 
- tool-call.start -> client receives immediate ack with call-id and preflight metadata
- tool-call.exec (optional progress deltas) -> server-side tool emits progress frames (tool-call.progress)
- tool-call.commit -> final result arrives as tool-result frame referencing call-id
- tool-call.error -> explicit error frames with structured error codes and recommended client behavior (retryable, idempotent, blocked)

4) Idempotency and resume: tool-call.start must include an optional client-provided idempotency_key so server-side retried invocations map to the same logical call and do not re-run irreversible actions. Resume tokens reference the last committed frame id and carry minimal state (model-version, active-tool-ids) to rehydrate session context.

API and SDK surface (developer ergonomics):

- Low-level: stream.on('frame', (f) => { /* raw envelope */ }) and helpers to filter by type. This is for advanced customers who want full control.

- High-level: an AsyncIterator that yields a typed stream of events (TextDelta, StructuredFragment, ToolCallEvent, ControlEvent). Example JS: for await (const evt of client.streamResponses(req)) { switch(evt.type) { case 'text_delta': ui.append(evt.text); break; case 'structured_fragment': builder.consume(evt.data); break; case 'tool_call_start': sdk.showToolModal(evt.callId, evt.meta); break; } }

- Builder helpers: SDKs must expose a small stateful builder that: assembles typed fragments into final objects; exposes an on('complete', obj) for structured outputs; and has safe APIs to dump a best-effort partial preview for UIs.

Developer ergonomics decisions:

- Default: SDKs will not attempt to auto-correct malformed fragments. They will surface a "fragment_error" event and provide a reassembly helper. Autocorrection is opt-in via an explicit config flag (auto_repair_fragments: true).

- Backpressure: SDKs will surface a simple flow control API: stream.pause(), stream.resume(), with built-in token-budget hints from the server (meta.token_hint). Mobile bindings must forward these hints to the hosting app so it can prioritize UI vs. tool execution.

- Offline fallback: SDKs include an offline simulator that replays server frames from a recorded transcript; this helps testing and onboarding.

Schema versioning and compatibility:

- Each frame includes schema_version and model_id. SDKs must expose the version to application code and enforce a stable minor/major compatibility policy: minor version changes are additive (safe); major changes require opt-in migration modes.

Observability and mapping to Console:

- Frame-level telemetry: frames must include trace_id, source (model|router|tool), and latency_ms. SDKs will bubble up a concise telemetry object for each frame that maps 1:1 to Console tiles.

- Error classification: produce structured error codes: transport_unavailable, tool_timeout, fragment_parse_error, idempotency_violation, schema_mismatch. Console will expose a filterable view.

Test plan and SDK conformance suite:

- A canonical test harness (hosted in repo) that runs a matrix of scenarios: intermittent network, progress-streaming tools, truncated fragments, duplicate tool-starts (idempotency), resume-after-crash.

- Contract tests: SDKs must pass an externally-run contract test that verifies: frame ordering, type separation, resume semantics, idempotency handling, and correct exposure of telemetry fields.

Rollout plan and compatibility strategy:

Phase 1 (Q1 2025): stabilize envelope and proto; ship reference JS SDK with builder and conformance tests. Beta with 5 partner customers.
Phase 2 (Q2 2025): Python + mobile SDKs, add Console mapping and telemetry dashboards. Provide migration guide for teams on Hosted and Dedicated.
Phase 3 (Q3 2025): make the protocol the recommended streaming surface; begin deprecation notices for older friction-prone patterns.

Operational considerations and security:

- Tool leakage: control frames must not leak sensitive tool metadata to unauthorized clients. Auth checks will be enforced at the control-plane before tool-call.start acks.

- Auditability: tool-call frames will be retained according to customer retention settings. Private deployments can opt for longer retention; Dedicated customers get a toggle.

Open questions and trade-offs:

- Do we include a standardized small binary codec (CBOR) option for mobile to reduce parsing cost? Trade-off: easier parsing vs. human-readable logs. Proposal: JSON-by-default, CBOR opt-in per connection.

- How aggressive should SDKs be about auto-repairing fragments? Conservative default recommended; allow opt-in heuristics library.

- Policy for tool-side side-effects on resume: require tools to implement idempotent handlers or mark calls as "no-resume" in preflight.

Next steps / immediate action items:

- Product to approve envelope minimal fields and error taxonomy (owner: Aisha).
- Engineering to produce a small reference JS library and the contract test harness (owner: Diego).
- DX to draft console tile mapping and telemetry event definitions (owner: Priya).
- Solutions to recruit 3 customers for beta and create onboarding checklist (owner: Evan).

Appendix: example frame sequence (human-readable)

1) {"t":"tool-call.start", "id":"c1", "p":{"tool":"search","query":"recent sales Q4"}, "meta":{"idempotency_key":"u-457"}}
2) {"t":"tool-call.progress", "id":"c1", "p":{"progress":20, "partial_results":[...]}}
3) {"t":"tool-call.commit", "id":"c1", "p":{"result":{"hits":[...]}, "status":"complete"}}
4) {"t":"delta", "id":"s1", "p":{"text":"Top results:\n1. ..."}}

This document is intended as a practical, developer-focused spec. Feedback requested on the envelope fields, telemetry mapping, and the idempotency/resume model.
